title: The Boat Under the Name
author: Lexi Zotomayor
imageAlt: A plank-built balangay boat, drawn in line
dek: Long before the galleons, boats sewn from planks carried people and goods across these islands. A note on the balangay of Butuan, and why it sails under this site's name.

bodyText:

The first thing you notice about a balangay is what it does not have. There are no nails. There is no keel in the way a European shipwright would mean it. There are planks, cut from a single log and shaped by hand, joined edge to edge with wooden pegs and lashed from the inside to ribs that were added after the hull was already a hull.

It is a boat built from the outside in. And for a long time it was how people in these islands moved: between rivers and coasts, between islands, and out into the wider sea.

## Found in a rice field

In 1976, people digging in Ambangan, in the barangay of Libertad in Butuan, struck wood. What they found turned out to be the remains of several plank boats, preserved for centuries in waterlogged ground. Archaeologists from the National Museum came, and over the years more boats were identified at the site.

The oldest of them has been dated to around the fourth century. Others are later, from the period when Butuan was a trading port that sent missions to China and dealt in gold, pottery and goods from across the region.

[Personal: when and how you first saw a balangay, or the replica, or the site. What struck you.]

## How a balangay was made

The method is called edge-joined, or plank-and-lug. Builders shaped each plank so that small raised lugs stood out from its inner face. Planks were fitted edge to edge and held with hardwood dowels. Then ribs were laid across the inside and tied to the lugs with fibre. The hull came first; the frame followed.

It sounds fragile. It was not. A boat like this could flex with the water instead of fighting it, and could be taken apart, repaired and put back together.

{{< pull cite="A boatbuilder's saying, often repeated" >}}The sea does not break what bends with it.{{< /pull >}}

## The word that stayed

Balangay is also the root of barangay, the smallest unit of local government in the Philippines today. The idea, often told, is that a boatload of families arriving together became a community on land, and kept the boat's name.

Historians argue about how literal that story is. But the word survived three centuries of Spain and half a century of America, and every Filipino address still carries it.

[Personal: your own barangay, or a memory of home that this connects to.]

## Sailing again

In 2009 a group of Filipino sailors and mountaineers built replica balangays using the old method and sailed them around the archipelago and on to neighbouring countries. They wanted to show that the boats could do what the records said they did.

They could.

## Why it is under the name

This site is called ditse, the word for the second-eldest sister: the one who is not quite in charge, but who remembers, and who tells you what happened when you were too young to notice. The balangay sails under the name because it is the oldest story I know about how we got here, and how we kept going.
